paragraphs.text: Lovers of Christ, I have marveled with you at the new things of the grace of the Gospel proclaimed through the Old Testament. With you my mind has been enlightened, as I watched the mark of the apostles shining out in the voices of the prophets. I acknowledge the gain, so that I may receive the reward. I have seen strange mysteries proclaimed through the Old Testament: Abraham taking an oath by his thigh, putting forward his thigh while calling the Maker of heaven and earth to witness his words. For he says, “Put your hand under my thigh, and swear to me by God, who made heaven and earth.” But a question arises. Suppose this was said on account of the seed that was to blossom from the thighs of Jacob, as in the words, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs.” How, then, will the oath turn out to be by the Savior? For Isaac had already been born, and the seed had already come forth, and when the oath was made there was no longer any hope of seed in Abraham's thigh. Abraham did have within himself the saving seed, of which Paul says, “It was said to Abraham and to his seed.” And weighing the wording and interpreting it, he says in the Letter to the Galatians, “It does not say, ‘And to your seeds,’ as of many, but, ‘And to your seed,’ who is Christ.” It has been shown, then, that Christ is the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, and so it was fitting that the oath was made by the seed. But the question is this: how could he swear by his thigh when the saving flower had already come forth? The answer is that once that member had become an instrument, and the divine seed had once dwelt there, he swears by it as by a temple. And whoever swears by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it. Who bears witness to this statement? Our Savior himself, when he says to the Pharisees, “Woe to you, foolish and blind Pharisees, for you say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’” And what does he say right after? “Foolish and blind! Which is greater, the gold, or the temple that has made the gold holy? Therefore I say to you: whoever swears by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it.”

A royal house, once it has received a king, a second or a third time, is set apart [?] once and for all because it once received a king, even if the king leaves the inhabited rooms. In the same way the patriarch's members, having once become instruments of the dispensation to come, were a temple of the promised blessing. So the oath is not wrongful, and the testimony is true. He makes the servant swear by the seed, and he explains what the seed is: "Put your hand under my thigh," he says, "and I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth." So our Savior is the God of heaven and earth. This is also why, in the prophet Zechariah, when various visions were sent and appeared to the holy man, this was one part of a vision: "And I lifted up my eyes," he says, "and looked, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, and seven lamps on top of the lampstand, and seven pourers for the lamps, and seven torches, and on the right of the lampstand and on the left two olive branches. And I said to the angel who was speaking with me: Lord, what are these?" It was a vision that showed one thing and led on to another for interpretation, and the things that appeared did not signify themselves but pointed to other things. So the prophet asks: "Lord, what are these?" If he had been asking about what appeared, he would have asked foolishly. Do you not know what a lampstand is, or an olive tree? But the prophet is not asking about what appears. He is asking about what is meant: "What are these?" And the angel says: "Do you not know what these are?" "No, lord." He frankly admits his ignorance and is taught by the truth. He too is a brother of the eunuch who heard from Philip: "Do you understand what you are reading?" And the eunuch frankly replied: "How can I, unless someone guides me?" "Do you not know what these are?" And he says: "No, lord." "What are the two olive branches on the right and on the left of the lampstand?" "These are the two sons of richness, who stand by the Lord of the whole earth." In explaining the olive trees, he also explains what the lampstand is.

Pay close attention. The lampstand was standing, and the branches were standing beside the lampstand. Yet when the angel interprets, he does not show the olive trees standing beside a lampstand. He shows them standing beside God. So the lampstand is a figure of God, or rather of our Savior and of his dispensation in the flesh. "Do you not know what these are?" "No, lord." "These branches are the two sons of richness, who stand by the Lord of the whole earth." They stand not by the lampstand, as it appears, but by the Lord of the whole earth. He presents a lampstand with seven lights because of the Lord's dispensation in the flesh. For the true lampstand was the Lord's flesh, which displayed the illuminations of the Holy Spirit in sevenfold grace. "For a rod shall come forth," says Isaiah, "from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him." Which Spirit? The one who is manifold in his workings and simple in his nature. "The Spirit of God shall rest upon him." Here he names the substance, the Holy Spirit himself. What follows speaks of the Spirit's workings: "the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, the spirit of the fear of God." These are the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, the seven workings that rested on the Lord's body, and he depicts them in the figure of lamps. And why seven lamps? Because the working of the Holy Spirit gives light. Then, going on further, he says again: "These are the seven eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth."

Do you see how the truth makes itself clear and has no need of human reasonings? But "they stand by the Lord of the whole earth." Zechariah calls the Savior Lord of the whole earth with reference to his dispensation in the flesh. Peter, the chief of the apostles, speaking with Cornelius, says: "We know the word that came to pass throughout Judea: Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit." And again the same apostle speaks of "the word throughout all Judea," and "the word which God sent, proclaiming peace to the children of Israel: he is Lord of all." The prophet says "Lord of the earth," and the evangelist Peter calls him "Lord of all." "He is Lord of all": of all things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, things visible and invisible. "He is Lord of all." So John speaks in harmony with this when he says: "He who comes from above is above all."

We must look into this carefully and settle the heretics' quarrel. They have followed the apostle's words wrongly. Instead of understanding them piously, they have twisted them impiously. So the children of heretics think that he received being above all things as a reward for the cross, and that God exalted him because he suffered and endured the cross. They follow the apostle's words without grasping their meaning, following the wording without examining the sense. The passage runs like this: "He humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him." Heretic, you are surely saying that God exalted him because of the passion, as if he had given him exaltation as the reward for his suffering. "And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth." "Do you see," he says, "that he was exalted after the cross? Do you see that he received exaltation as a reward after the passion?" Well then, if he was exalted after the cross, as you claim, why did John the Baptist say before the passion and before the cross: "He who comes from above is above all"? He did not say "becomes." That is also why Jesus said to the Jews: "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am." For he always is, and was, and will be, and will have no end. But, brothers, we must pay our debt and not use our digressions as an excuse to go back on our promises. Let the glory of Christ be proclaimed, and the majesty of the Father. Let the Holy Spirit be proclaimed, let the Only-begotten be exalted, let the Father be glorified. Let no one think that their dignity is overturned if we mention the Spirit first, then the Son, then the Father, or the Son first, or the Father. The divine nature has no order. This is not because it is disordered. It is because it transcends order. God is not a shape, not because he is shapeless, but because he lies beyond shape. God has no form, not because he is formless, but because he is bodiless. In the same way the divine nature has no order, not because it is disordered, but because it transcends order.

I speak of the Father as first, not first in order but first in our thinking, since he is the begetter of the Only-begotten, the root of the holy fruit, eternal light from which eternal light is begotten. My brothers, suppose someone among us tried today, in church, among an orthodox people filled with all right knowledge, to place the Son before the Father. Would the orthodox themselves not call it blasphemy? Suppose someone dared to say in church, "Christ and his Father will bless you." Would he not be thought disorderly, for failing to put the root first and then bring in the fruit? Suppose someone said, "The Son and the Father will save us." Would he not be thought to cause confusion and break the order? Unfair judges would think so. But when truth sits as judge and the apostle's vote carries the day, it makes no difference whether the Son, the Father or the Spirit is mentioned first. Listen to how Paul, the great herald, puts it when he writes to the Thessalonians: "Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father sanctify us." The Son is first and the Father second. O soul filled with the holy torch! This shows that there is no order in the holy nature. Whichever is placed first is understood to be of equal honor, the second is not diminished, and the third is not insulted. So he puts the names forward without distinction, because he knows the nature is undivided and the kingdom unsevered. Let us ask holy Paul where he found the grounds for speaking of God this way, for giving glory this way, for placing the Son before the Father, not in order or in power but in the wording. Why did he mention the Son first and then the Father? Let Paul speak in his own defense and teach the Church: "I say nothing of my own. Christ dictates the doctrines through me. Or are you seeking proof that Christ is speaking in me? Christ speaks through me. Do not accuse me. Do not find fault with the Lord's voice. But can you not grasp that Christ is speaking through me? Then listen to him speaking openly in his own person." Suppose the names of the Holy Trinity were subject to order, so that the one named first was first in power, the second was second in rank, and the third was third by being lesser. Would the Savior, who is himself the truth, then have confused the account of the truth? And where did the Savior mention himself first and then the Father? "If anyone keeps my commandments," he says, "I and the Father will come and make our home with him."

"Now here," say the children of heretics, "he went beyond the proper order." They want the Son to be to the Father something like a prefect to a king. Let them be asked whether a prefect ever dared to say of a king, "I and the king decree." Understand the things above us from the things that belong to us. Would a created nature put itself before the uncreated? Would a created nature, as you call it, have dared to count itself alongside that incomparable supremacy and say, "We will come and make our home with him"? No. By saying "I and the Father" he showed that the names are interchangeable, and by saying "We will come and make our home" he showed that their working is equal in honor. So too in another passage, when the apostle Philip says, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us," the Savior answers: "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?" The answer seems to go against the question. "Was I asking about you? I said, 'Show us the Father.'" But he says: "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?" If the Son were unlike the Father, how could the unlike be shown through what is unlike? How could the great be seen through the small? How could the one who excels in dignity be seen through the lesser, or the creator through the servant? "Have I been with you so long?" He did not say, "The Father is with you," but "I am." For where I am, the Father is. "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?" "You have not known me" is well said. Philip says "Show," and the Savior says "You have not known me?" He wants to show that God is made present by knowledge, not by sight. "Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?" Again he says "I" first, and then "the Father." "I am in the Father and the Father is in me. How then can you say, 'Show us the Father'?" This means: How could you expect to see him as someone other than me? "I am in the Father and the Father is in me," and the Son is known through the Father and the Father through the Son. "How can you say 'Show us,' as if you were seeking to see the Father as someone apart from me? I am in the Father and the Father is in me." This does not mean that the nature is confused, or that one is placed inside the other like a cup inside a cup. "I am in the Father and the Father is in me." He is not speaking of bodies joined together. This is something perceived by the mind.

"I am in the Father," for the Father is not known without the Son, "and the Father is in me," for the Son does not appear without the Father. In the same way the mind is perceived in the word and the word in the mind. How can I know your thought except through what you say? Your word presents your mind, and your mind in turn interprets your word. One cannot perceive a word without grasping the thought, or grasp the thought unless the word has expressed it. That is why the evangelist says, "In the beginning was the Word": to show that the begetting involved no passion. What a word is to the mind, the only-begotten Word is to the Father. And here is the wonderful thing. Let me take up again something said earlier. It was said before that you will learn what the things above us are like from the things that belong to us. When a word is within, together with the mind that begot it, is it visible together with something visible? No. It is invisible with the invisible, intelligible with the intelligible, bodiless with the bodiless. But when the word is about to come forth, it moves to the mouth, and there it clothes itself in voice. No other nature supplies it with the voice. The word itself weaves its own speech. So too the one who is invisible in nature together with the Father came forth clothed in a voice, and he who was hidden before became plain to all. Then, having come forth, he fills all things, yet he does not depart from the mind that begot him.

What person, when he speaks a word and teaches others, empties himself of the word? If I say something and it reaches other people's ears, has it left my mind empty? Has the word not gone out and yet stayed within? Has it not filled countless ears without withdrawing from the one who begot it? Now the human word, sent out by the one who begot it, both goes out and does not leave its begetter behind. Did God the Word, then, leave the Father's bosom empty when he appeared in the world for our sake? By no means. And here is the wonderful thing. Tens of thousands hear the one Word of God. He reaches so many and yet is not divided. He is wholly with each of us who hear, and wholly with all. Did the Father then beget by flowing out and cutting off, and was he split and divided, as they say? Let the Savior say to them: "Search the Scriptures." Search them, do not corrupt them. Search them, not merely reading them but tracking down the depths of their meaning. God gave the Scriptures, but he did not lay their meanings bare. He left them to your own pursuit, to test your good sense and see your zeal, to see whether you serve the Scriptures or do violence to them. God set before us the nature of things but hid the arts. Everything was put forth by God, but craft was born of human thought. It is the same with the Scriptures.

Let me make this clear. God gave stones. He gave the nature of stones, not a finished building. He gave wheat, not bread. He gave the grape cluster, not wine. He gave the nature of wool, not a garment. He gave earth that yields gold, but not gold itself. Why? Because he makes man in God's image, he shares the work of creation with him. God himself creates, and through man's skill he gives shape to what he has created. Because he makes man after his own image, he shares with him the nobility of what has come into being. He works as creator, and as God, having brought all things from nothing into being, he himself brings in the nature that did not exist. But he leaves it to his image to adorn what has been made. Think who the man was who first put together a plow. How did he think to cut the wood, set iron in the middle, bind it together, devise a yoke, true its lines and bring the oxen together? There was wood and there was iron, but there was no craft. Who told you, man, that this is how a plow is put together? Who suggested to you that the unyielding nature of iron could be softened by fire? Who showed you how to make a tiny needle from such a coarse mass? Who conceived in his mind how to make doorways out of stones? Where did you learn how to design roofs? Tell me, man. "You are greatly astonished," he says, "because you have no experience. You are looking at the image of God, and you ask how it learned?"

So, brothers, human nature everywhere imitates its Master and adorns nature with craft. As long as it imitates within measure, it is good. When it goes beyond measure, its excess brings it disgrace. For example, it worked out how to subdue the ox, the horse, the camel and all the irrational creatures that were given for its service. But out of greed it devised mixing things against nature. It crossed the donkey with the horse. God did not want this. From the beginning he had said: "Let the earth bring forth four-footed animals and creeping things according to their kind." But greed mixed things against nature. God punished the excess by making the invention barren. That is why the mule does not bear young: it is not one of those creatures made back then that heard, "Increase, and fill the earth." Yet even before the image acts, God allows it to do what it wishes, so as to show its power and to punish its excess.

Again, the excess of desire set out to make a human form, imitating, as it supposes, God at work. It makes an image of a body and forces nature by craft. Craft had heard that God made man and fashioned him from earth. Unable to imitate its Master in truth, it finds ways to do the impossible through its inventions. It gathers roots and mixes colors. It imitates an eye that is open and looks but does not see, an ear spread wide but not hearing, nostrils drawn straight up but unable to draw breath, a mouth shaped but deprived of voice, feet well proportioned but with no fitness for running. God allowed this to show what he had granted to the image, as if to say, "so that my own working may be shown." He did not allow it to lay hold of everything, lest it fall into arrogance and give up on itself and its own salvation. Yet he allowed painters to make figures from earth, to shame those who deny that God fashioned man from earth. Another craft imitated the Creator. It saw a body cut by iron, for instance where part of the flesh was cut away by a blade. The hollow must be filled up, and the eaten-away flesh must be built up again. The craftsman is not a creator who can fashion flesh. What then? The craft of the image, imitating the nature of its Master, hurried to the earth from which the body came. It prepares medicines and makes plasters. One cleanses, the other builds up.

And see the wonderful thing. God sits like a father and a teacher, watching the works of his own image. A father asks his son, "What does this idea mean?" He does this not to learn but to test him. In the same way, the source of all good things is always teaching its own image and setting problems before it. He brought the irrational animals and the birds to Adam "to see what he would call them." He who knows all things beforehand did this not to learn, but to test whether the image was fit for understanding. In came building. Then came carpentry, seafaring, smithing, tailoring, and the study of the stars. This was not the meddlesome kind but the kind that observes their positions, which is useful to sailors, watches the risings of the stars and recognizes the season for good sailing. It was not the kind that invents horoscopes and spins tales about fate, but the kind that follows the Master's word: "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them be for signs and for days and for seasons."

The image went forth and explores nature. It looks for herbs and finds them. It seeks out roots and discovers them. It proves to be the craftsman and inventor of everything. But so that it would not think it had found these things by itself, and not by the power of the one who put that power into its nature, God shows in a single passage that he is the teacher of our nature in all these things. Blessed Solomon came forward and said: "For he himself gave me unerring knowledge of what exists: to know the structure of the world and the working of the elements, the beginning and end and middle of times, the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars, the natures of living creatures and the tempers of wild beasts, the varieties of plants and the powers of roots. All things hidden and manifest I came to know, I, man, the image." How did you come to know them? "For wisdom, the craftswoman of all things, taught me." She taught you what is within measure, not what is beyond measure. For see how human craft, though it was the image of God, poured itself out into many excesses. It studied how the organ of the voice produces sound, and by observing nature it imitates nature with craft. It devises the sound of the organ, the instrument of many pipes, woven together from many reeds. See what it does, and how precisely craft has fitted itself to nature. It devised bellows, which do not bring forth breath from themselves but expand and borrow air from elsewhere. Then it sent the air from the two bellows into a wind chest and on into all the pipes. It contrived that the air should flow and yet there should be no sound until a finger shaped the note. Where did this come from, man? How did you build an instrument and a reservoir for air? Why does the flowing air make no sound while the pipes stand open? "You are greatly astonished," he says, "because you have no experience. I told you before: I am the image of God. I looked at my own nature and imitated myself." How did you imitate yourself? "I saw this same borrowed breath in myself as well. My chest constantly expands and contracts and takes in the inflow of air. I see two windpipes sending on the air. It passes to the mouth as through a pipe. I see that the air goes forth, yet no word is formed unless the tongue shapes the sound. I looked at myself and emulated myself. From myself I grasped the Master's craft, as David says: 'Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me.' I looked at myself and praised the craftsman. I imitated my own Master. By craft I represented nature."

For the instrument is not bad in itself; but when it becomes an instrument of shameful songs ... [?] if they had been called divine, as they were from the beginning, they would not be profane, even if, in their excess, they were invented for luxury. Still, if they had been consecrated to God, as they were from the beginning, they would not be profane. That is why David says: "Praise him with psaltery and lyre, praise him with strings and organ, praise him with well-sounding cymbals, praise him with cymbals of jubilation, praise him with timbrel and dance." If only the invention had not been turned to licentious luxury or to the worship of idols! If it had offered to God the fruits of what it invented, no one would have blamed the art for its invention. If the lyre had acknowledged its Master, no one would have blamed it. If only God were proclaimed through the lyre! This is why it happened with blessed David. He made himself a lyre, and with it he did not sing shameful songs but sent up holy words, so the lyre became both consecrated to God and a means of putting demons to flight. For when a demon struck King Saul, battered him and threw him to the ground, whenever, it says, blessed David struck up the lyre, Saul grew well and found relief. Do you see that no art would have anything bad in it if it were tuned to please God? Instead, everything would have turned out for us as we wished.

But what was my purpose in coming from theology to art and the imitation of the image? It was to turn the Lord's words against the heretics. Which words? "Hypocrites, you know how to interpret the face of the sky and of the earth." You have discovered arts and thought up many inventions, and yet you insult the Master and Craftsman of all? You imitated the Master by your art, and you were promised that you would be like him, "after the image and likeness"; and do you proclaim that I, the Creator, am unlike the one who begot me? I set you free when you were subject to sin; and do you summon me, the Master of all, to be subject? "Yes," he says, "for it is written: 'And the Son himself will be subjected.'" It is indeed said, but in a sense fitting God. For what is said is not our own; it is God's message that is being proclaimed. Then, to follow the wording ... I allow those who have heard to know what is meant. [?] So, to follow the wording: in the creation to come, in the resurrection, he will be subjected then, while you become then equal to the angels? For "in the resurrection of the dead," says the Savior, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God." Are you raised up from your own rank, while the Son comes down from lordship into subjection? Have you not heard Paul saying, "For the creation was subjected to vanity, because the creation itself groans together until now"? "The creation": which one? Heaven, earth and everything else. "For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly." To what vanity? To human vanity. Why does he call man vanity? Because man turned away from the image to become like the irrational beasts. "For vanity of vanities, all is vanity." And David says: "Surely all things are vanity, every man living." It was to this vanity, then, to man in his corruption, that the creation was subjected. How was it subjected? The sun rises on the unworthy, the springs gush for the ungrateful, the earth bears its fruit for the thankless. So the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly. For if it had been up to its own choice, it would not willingly have been subjected to the unworthy; it was "because of him who subjected it." And for what purpose is it subjected? "In hope." What hope? "That the creation itself" (Paul is the one saying this) "will be set free from its bondage to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God." Is the creation set free at that time, while the Son is reduced to slavery?

"Search the Scriptures"; do not slander. "Search"; do not meddle. "Search" in faith, not in contradiction. Where did you learn to say, "Was he begotten when he was, or when he was not?" Where did you learn to say, "To beget and to create are the same thing with God"? Did Peter teach you this? Did Paul suggest it? Did the Savior hand these things down to you? Read the Scripture and respect the law. Yet he does not even stand by what he himself says. For when he asks, "Was he begotten when he was, or when he was not?" he is lying, since he is examining something he does not confess. First confess that he was begotten, and then ask whether it was when he was or when he was not. You deny the fact, and then you torture the word? If you do not grant that he was begotten, why do you inquire into his begetting? "Was he begotten when he was, or when he was not?" Grant that he was begotten. First establish that he was begotten, and then inquire. You deny the nature and examine the wording? Are creating and begetting the same thing? Where does the Son come from? Let one of them tell me. Unless the order of the two is clear first, and the meaning then agrees, I cannot say, "To see and to look are the same," for I have said only one thing. But if I say, "To hear and to see are the same," then I seem to be saying that things which differ, not in sight [?] but agreeing in hearing [?], are the same with God. How do you know that creating and begetting are the same? If he both begot and created, you are right to say they are the same. But if, as you claim, he never begot but only created, how can begetting and creating be the same? This is vainglory in words, words empty of the truth of things.

Why do they spin sophistries about begetting and creating? "God," he says, "is simple, and not as we are. We beget with one part and create with another; for instance, we beget with the organs of generation but create with the hand. God is not like that," he says, "for he is simple and without form. In whatever way he begets, in that same way he also creates." Since you make pronouncements about invisible things, puffed up by this ill-timed and empty philosophy, let one of the visible things convince you that things done in the same way do not [?] have the same meaning. Take this hand of mine, which can be seen, so that the refutation of what is invisible may proceed from what is visible. This hand is one in itself, yet it does different things, and what it accomplishes cannot be brought under a single view. For example, with the same hand I create and I overturn. Then, since creating and overturning are done by the same hand, are they the same? No, they are not the same. Since they say, "We beget in one way and create in another," I say in turn: I create in the same way, with the same hand, that I also tear down. With the same hand I both strike and heal. Will striking and healing then be the same? With the same hand I both push down the one who stands and raise up the one who has fallen. With the same hand I both cast a vote and annul the vote. Will casting a vote and annulling it then be the same? Is this not beyond foolish talk? Are these not fables and absurdities? Does not Paul's soul groan, is not Peter indignant, when such people run riot against the divine teaching? You have renounced what belongs to Christ and learned what belongs to others. Have you not heard the Lord saying, "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words"? Many often confess Christ but are ashamed of his words. The heretic confesses Christ, but when he comes to speak of Father and Son, he is ashamed of the term and says, "Did the one who cannot suffer beget? Then it was by an outflowing! Then it was by making!" Do you see that you are ashamed of the term? What folly! They have become hunters of words, not careful examiners of their meaning. For vanity has corrupted everything.

As I have often said, the origins and sources of the heretics are plain to see. If the Church holds a heretical teaching, name the founder of what we have stated. Who gave birth to this "heresy" of ours, as you call it? The apostles proclaimed it from the beginning. After the apostles, the synod at Nicaea confirmed it. And to show that this was the faith of the whole world: out of so many who gathered, only seven dissented, and they were condemned. The whole world agreed as one, because it came from the apostolic dough.

And see what a wonder this is. By God's design the New imitated the Old. When the kings of the Assyrians came against the land of Palestine, Abraham went out against the foreigners, against five kings. The man of faith went out alone. And how many servants did he lead out against them? Three hundred and eighteen, born in his house. As many as Abraham led out against the foreigners, so many did Christ also lead out against the heresies. As many as Abraham led out against the foreigners, or rather enlisted to fight alongside him, so many did Christ also arm alongside himself against the heresies. There were three hundred and eighteen bishops at Nicaea; and there, three hundred and eighteen servants of Abraham born in his house. Why did it say "born in his house"? Because he also had slaves bought with money; but it showed the true members of the household. And now Christ led out, not just anyone at all, but those born in his house, who proclaim him who is from him who is, the living from the living, light from light.

Why do you say "light" and "light"? What difference is there between life and life? What is the distinction? And here is the wonder: the Father was called light, but the Son with an addition. John the evangelist says of the Father, "God is light," but of the Son, "He was the true light." The Father was called light without qualification, since the audacity of heretics does not readily make war on the Father's divinity, although the outrages they dare against Christ carry the insult up to the Father too. Nevertheless, Scripture establishes what is agreed with a simple statement, but fortifies what is disputed with the truth. The Father is light, without addition, for it is enough for him to be proclaimed in order to be known. The Son is light; but so that no one may say, "That one is spiritual light, but this other is spurious," he is "true light." Again, someone might say: just as the sun is light and the moon is light, but one is a great light and the other a small light, so too the Father is light, but great, and the Son is light, but small. To keep him from saying this, Isaiah anticipates him: "Land of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light." If God is light, and a great light, God is great. If God is light, as John wrote, "God is light," and if God is the great light, then the Son too is great God. Great is the one who begot and great the one begotten; great the root, great the fruit; great the light, and great too the radiance. I know of no small and great; I know one great God, the Trinity. God is great: "the great, the eternal God," says Isaiah; and Paul says: "awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." "Great is God, great is our Lord," as David says, "and great is his strength." But since strength and power are the same ... [?] for "Christ is the power of God." "Great is our Lord": as if he were saying, Great is the Father, great is his Power. "Great is our Lord, and great is his strength." Great strength, since the Holy Spirit too is great power, as the Savior says to the apostles: "Stay in Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high."

But see what sophistries they devise about the power. "The power," he says, "is something that holds the promise of wealth [?]. For the Spirit is not called God," he says, "but a pledge from God." And hear how he argues: "A pledge is part of a gift, not the whole gift but a part of the whole. For it is written," he says, "by the apostle: 'You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance.' See," he says, "that he is a gift of God, and not God. So then he is a gift and a pledge, a part of the whole." Well then, if you find God too called a portion and not the whole, and a gift and not the whole, what will you do? For it says, "the pledge of the inheritance." What is the pledge? What is the inheritance? What is "the pledge of the inheritance"? The inheritance is a gift from the one who has given it, not the very one who is inherited. So it says: the Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance. If the Spirit's being called a pledge offends your soul, what do you do when you find God called an inheritance? Pay close attention to how he is called not only the one inherited, but even himself an inheritance. Hear David saying: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." God is "the portion of my inheritance"; the Spirit is "the pledge of the inheritance." If being called "the portion of the inheritance" makes the Father lesser, then being called "the pledge of the inheritance" also lessens the dignity of the Spirit. Elsewhere David says: "Lord, you are my portion in the land of the living." "My portion": who did the apportioning? For if he is one part, he is not the whole. If you are a hunter of words and not an examiner of meanings, nothing stops you from blaspheming even the Father, whom you think you revere. "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance," and "Lord, you are my portion in the land of the living." Why, then, is the self-existent Power called portion and inheritance? Because we receive God by our own choice. Each of us chooses: one chooses error, another receives God, and the God he has chosen becomes the believer's portion. Here is an example of what I mean. It is written to the Levites: "You shall have no portion in the land, for the Lord is their portion." If God's being called a portion does not offend you, why does the Holy Spirit's being called a pledge offend you?

Let us strip away all the confusion of unbelief and receive the faith that is free of confusion. How long, heretic, will you harden your heart like Pharaoh? How long will you refuse to weigh the divine words in the balance? You have reason within you as a balance: weigh the Savior's words. Consider which words concern the flesh and which concern the divinity. Consider what concerns his dignity and what concerns the dispensation, so that what the prophet says about Canaan may not be said of you as well: "Canaan: in his hand is a balance of injustice; he loved to oppress." And David says: "But the sons of men," that is, the heretics, "are vain in the balance, to do injustice." Do you hold a balance and corrupt justice? Look at the Savior's balance: "I and the Father are one." Where is the inequality? Look at the scales of God the Word: "He who has seen me has seen the Father." Where is the pan that sinks, where the one that rises? See the Father setting free and the Son setting free, as he himself says, "Unless the Son sets you free, you are slaves," and as Paul says, "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free." If the Father sets free, if the Son sets free, if the Spirit sets free, where is the slave? But may all of us escape the yoke of sin and the yoke of heresy and hold to the faith unswervingly.

And let the heretics not be ignorant of what is said. For I have heard many people asking, "Why does he not speak to us about morals? Why not about conduct and decency?" They do not say this out of longing for it, but to escape being refuted. Do you want true correction? You have often heard the great teaching. You have heard about morals: correct your morals. You have heard about conduct: set your conduct in order. But it is just as the Lord said: "John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, 'He has a demon'; the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, 'A glutton and a drunkard.'" Nothing pleases wickedness. If you speak about morals, it says, "I am asking about the faith." If you speak about the faith, it says, "I wanted to hear about conduct." That is why the Savior, rebuking the childishness of wickedness, said: "We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not beat your breasts." We piped for you with a holy word, with a word full of light, about the right ordering of morals, and you did not listen. We mourned with a word full of toil and grief, lamenting your unbelief, and you did not listen. Neither did you dance when you heard what concerned you, nor did you grieve when you heard what was said against the heresies.

The Baptist came, and they say, "He has a demon." And the Baptist is not indignant, but keeps to his work. Do you see that he suffers the same things as the Savior? The Jews said of the Savior, "He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?" Is not a Christian blessed who falls under the same insult as his Master? Paul preaches the truth, and Festus says to him, "You are mad, Paul; your great learning is driving you mad." For sober things look like madness to those who are not in their right mind. But he says, "I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking words of soberness and justice." You see the God-inspired boldness that was taken for madness, yet shone brighter than sobriety. John the Baptist hears, "You have a demon," just as the prophets of old heard that they were possessed.

Once the prophet Elisha sent one of his own disciples, a prophet, and said to him: "Go, and you will find Jehu the commander. Take him aside and say to him, 'Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I have anointed you king.' And pour the horn of oil on him and anoint him king." The prophet sends a disciple who is a prophet. He takes the commander, for Jehu was not king at that time, but a commander under the reigning king. He says to him, "Come aside." And taking him aside, he speaks the words and anoints him from the horn. And when he had anointed him, he fled; he went away. Jehu's companions say to him, "Why did this madman come to you?" that is, "Why did this demoniac come?" "Why did this madman come to you?" So from the beginning the prophets were insulted, and so were the apostles. "Why did this madman come to you?" Jehu, afraid that he might spread abroad the word of kingship and put himself in danger (for while a king is reigning, it is dangerous for the rule to pass to another), says, "You know his babbling and his nonsense." He agreed with them, not in his mind but with his voice: "You know his babbling." Then, realizing that the truth is never a laughing matter, the very men who had mocked are eager to learn the truth: "It is not right, Jehu, if you do not tell us. You are wronging your friends; you do wrong to hide the secret." If he is a madman, why do you want to hear the madman's words? "You do wrong, Jehu, if you do not tell us." Wickedness despises what belongs to virtue, yet is in anguish over it. They condemned him as possessed, and at the same time scrutinized his words as true. "Tell us what he told you." "He took me aside." See the strength of the truth: how the glory that was laughed at came to be revered, how the madman of a prophet proved stronger even than laws. He says, "He took me aside and poured the horn of oil on me." And the commanders raised their voices, saying, "Long live the king!" Do you see how at one and the same moment they laughed at the prophecy and marveled at it, condemned it and believed it? You called him possessed, and do you call the man he appointed king?

So neither we, nor our fathers, nor those who come after us should be surprised if we hear from a heretical tongue anything meant to insult us. May it be ours to be insulted for Christ, so that we may be glorified in Christ, both now and in the rest that awaits us there; to whom...
